title: Blessings for wonders
hookLine: there are blessings for lightning, thunder, the sea, a rainbow and trees in blossom
carry: the world has blessings built in
last: YOU KEPT ME ALIVE FOR THIS.

cards: You're driving home in a summer storm. The sky goes white for half a second, and the counting starts: one Mississippi, two Mississippi. Then the thunder rolls over the car.
Or a beach at the end of a long drive, and there it is, the whole sea at once. Or a rainbow, and everyone in the parking lot pulls out a phone. Nobody plans these moments.
Jewish tradition wrote blessings for many of them anyway, ready before they arrive. Today: ma'aseh vereishit.

teach.b: The Mishnah, the early collection of rabbinic law, lists them, and the Talmud and later law sort out the endings. Each starts with the six words.
In common practice, for lightning and for great mountains: oseh ma'aseh vereishit, who makes the work of creation. As if the world is still being made, right now, in front of you.

For thunder, and in the Mishnah's list also earthquakes and fierce winds: shekocho u'gevurato malei olam, whose strength and might fill the world. For the great sea, seen after a long while: who made the great sea.
For a rainbow, a blessing that remembers the promise after the flood: who remembers the covenant, is faithful to it, and keeps his word.
The story in Genesis says, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "I have set My bow in the cloud." Some even teach not to stare at a rainbow too long, out of respect.

teach.h: TREES IN BLOSSOM, ONCE A YEAR.
teach.b: And once a year, in the spring month of Nisan, on first seeing fruit trees in blossom, there's a blessing for God, who left nothing lacking in the world, and created good creatures and good trees for people to enjoy.
Some go out looking for a blossoming tree just to say it.
A psalm names what they share: "How manifold are Thy works, O LORD! In wisdom hast Thou made them all." And a quiet point hides inside the list. Nobody schedules lightning.
The words are ready before the storm comes, so the surprise and the answer can arrive together.

how: Jews say short blessings on seeing lightning, hearing thunder, seeing the sea or a rainbow, and once a year on seeing fruit trees in blossom in the spring month of Nisan.

o: a blessing said before eating bread
the name of a week-long harvest festival
the work of creation, still being made right now

games.q: which wonder gets which words — tap the pairs.
p: who makes the work of creation

s: the rainbow blessing recalls the promise after the flood
"I have set My bow in the cloud": who remembers the covenant and keeps his word.
the blessing for blossoming trees is said every day
once a year, in the spring month of Nisan, on first seeing fruit trees in blossom.
the blessing for the great sea is said every time you see it
it's for seeing the great sea after a long while, not every glance.

games.q: you're outside when a rainbow appears. everyone is snapping pictures. what does Jewish tradition suggest?
o: stare at it as long as you can.
say its blessing, and don't stare too long.
games.why: say the blessing for the one who remembers the covenant, and some teach not to gaze at it too long, out of respect.

practice: Look out a window if there is one, or close your eyes and listen: the sky, a cloud, a tree, a bird, the light on a wall, rain. Let something ordinary surprise you, as if you'd never seen it.
If you pray, offer one of the old endings, who makes the work of creation; if you don't, simply say wow, and mean it.

wordCard.voice: Ma'aseh vereishit. The work of creation, the phrase opening the blessing for lightning and great mountains, as if the world is still being made, right now.

orig.note: Hebrew: who makes the work of creation, said on seeing lightning and other wonders of nature.

carryVoice: Your line: the world has blessings built in. Lightning, seas, rainbows, blossoms, each with its own words. Until tomorrow.
